speaker: Doctor
text: I am Dr. Agent. I see you are evaluating a newborn with respiratory distress. To begin, I need to know the gestational age at birth and if there were any complications during delivery, such as meconium-stained amniotic fluid or maternal fever.

speaker: Patient
text: Newborn, born at 33 weeks of gestation. The newborn is presenting with respiratory distress 2 hours after birth. The mother had an uneventful pregnancy until premature onset of labor. There was no significant prenatal care history mentioned.

speaker: Doctor
text: The baby is premature at 33 weeks with no prior complications, which strongly points toward a surfactant deficiency. Can you describe the specific signs of respiratory distress, such as grunting, nasal flaring, or retractions, and what the oxygen saturation levels are?

speaker: Patient
text: My main symptom is Respiratory distress. I also have Grunting, Intercoastal and subcostal retractions, Peripheral cyanosis.

speaker: Doctor
text: The clinical picture of a 33-week preterm infant with grunting, retractions, and cyanosis is classic for Respiratory Distress Syndrome due to surfactant deficiency. To confirm this, I need to see the radiographic evidence of diffuse ground-glass opacities and air bronchograms. REQUEST TEST: Chest_X-Ray

speaker: Measurement
text: RESULTS: Fine reticular granulation with ground glass appearance on both lungs

speaker: Doctor
text: The chest X-ray confirms the diagnosis with fine reticular granulation and a ground-glass appearance, which is pathognomonic for surfactant deficiency. DIAGNOSIS READY: Neonatal Respiratory Distress Syndrome
